utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I take once again the opportunity to remind you that you are bound by the declaration you made on the first day you came to give evidence, to make -- to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I have been abiding by that so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony yesterday, and I believe even the day before, you testified that the JNA was comprised of individuals from all different ethnic groups, that it was a multi-ethnic army and not a Serb army. Isn't it true, though, that by September of 1991, that had changed and that all of the military district and operational group commanders were in fact Serb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Whiting, the fighting around Vukovar continued even after the date you mention. The commander of the first army was still General Spirkovski, a Macedonian. The commander of the air force was a Croat, Zvonko Jurjevic, and the period you're referring to is subsequent to the date you mentioned. My friend told me, for instance, that the entire artillery battery at Vukovar was composed of Croats from Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned Aleksandar Spirkovski. In fact, he was -- he was replaced as the first military district commander in September of 1991 and he was replaced by Zivota Panic in September of 1991 and Mr. Panic is a Serb; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. He is Serb, but the Prime Minister was a Croat and he probably made an influence over these changes. He had an influence over these changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That wasn't responsive to the question, sir. The -- isn't it true that in September of 1991, Mr. Spirkovski was replaced and Zivota Panic, who you can -- say was a Serb, replaced him, isn't that true, in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't tell whether this was in September. I do believe you but I told you that Zivota Panic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the other commanders in Vukovar, Mile Mrksic, Andrija Biorcevic were also Serbs, isn't that true? Certainly after September 1991, if not before, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't know whether Andrija is a Serb. I can't tell. The other two you mentioned, I know are Serbs but these were people holding junior commanding positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But they were commanders in Vukovar; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have agreed with you. I said that the only point that I wanted to make was that they were lower-ranking compared to the other ones we were mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you also testified about -- you said that there were a number of cease-fire violations that were committed by the Croatian side. It's true, isn't it, that cease-fire violations were also committed by the Serb side during the time that you were Foreign Minister and afterwards, isn't that also -- isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, at government meetings, we issued strict instructions to the effect that the peace process should not be interrupted, that Croats should not be attacked. However we received information that every time that there had been shooting at the border or one of the sides opening fire, it was always the Croats. I told you that this was stage-managed by them in order to convince the journalists or diplomats, whoever they brought over there, that it was the Serbs who started the violations of cease-fires first. However, in the UN Security Council's documents, the situation reflected there was not the accurate one. The documents produced by Nambiar because they wanted to present the situation in a different manner. The Croats wanted to present it in the way it suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, would you please now answer the question. We are thankful for the speech you made. Can you please now answer the question. Do you want to be reminded of the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it true that there were also cease-fire violations committed by Serbs? Yes or no. We've heard your speech. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you were Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether someone on the Serb side had gone against the government instructions. It may have happened locally. However, the army and the police of the RSK had never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Thank you for that speech. Please answer the question. Is it true that while you were Foreign Minister, Serbs also violated cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was clear about that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But going back to the -- something you said earlier, I just want to see if I understand what you said clearly. Did you state that largely it was the Croatian side that violated the cease-fire agreements and that if the internationals who were present say otherwise, it was because they were tricked by the Croatians? You talked about it being stage-managed and is that -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not clear on what the answer you've just given. I had understood your answer earlier to be that it was the Croatian side, as you knew, it was the Croatian side that was violating the cease-fire agreements but that the international representatives were deceived into believing that it was the Serbs. Did I understand what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me correctly. I spoke of two different situations. They didn't bring over UNPROFOR officers to deceive them but diplomats, representatives of international organisations, and they wanted to show them that allegedly it was the Serb who is were the first ones to violate the cease-fire agreement. Secondly, as far as UNPROFOR representatives are concerned, I said clearly that before leaving for India, General Nambiar told me, hesitatingly, although probably he felt compelled to say that, that none of the unfavourable documents for Croats were able to enter Croatia so the documents you have are actually only partly accurate because they conceal the evil that the Croats committed on their part. I've been repeating this several times, and I hope that this Trial Chamber will be satisfied of that as the Defence will be leading documents here proving that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, before you proceed with answering the next question for Mr. Whiting, I thought that you were also saying that Croats within the JNA were responsible for certain infractions and these were being put forward as having been committed by Serbs. Is that also your evidence or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't understand your question fully. If we are discussing the JNA and officers of the JNA, we have to know the time period we are referring to. Of course, that there was a certain point in time when all the Croats had left the JNA except for some honourable exceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The period that was being referred to was whilst you were the Foreign Minister. Are you saying at that time that all Croats would have left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, when I became Foreign Minister, and that was in October 1992, all of the Yugoslav army was in the territory of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. It could not be discussed any longer in terms of being in the territory of the RSK. It had already withdrawn from Bosnia after having been attacked and after the JNA soldiers and officers had been massacred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We leave it at that for the time being, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I will also leave this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you some questions about the negotiations that you spoke about. You testified on the first day of your evidence that you went to New York for negotiations in January of 1993. And we saw at the beginning of the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in February of 1993. And we saw in the beginning of your -- the cross-examination, the statements that were made by your delegation before leaving for New York or made on behalf of your 4 delegation. You also testified and this is at page 43 of the first day of your testimony, that nothing was accomplished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you? Mr. Jarcevic, are you well? Are you okay? Are you okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I am. I feel well. I explained to you yesterday that I'm a bit upset about the fact that 20 years later, the world still fails to understand what happened in the former Yugoslavia. I'm sensitive person, I'm one of the few people who survived in the area I hail from. 270 of my fellow peers were killed. Therefore, I am upset. But believe me, I am in good health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may be so, sir. You see, the fact that you told us yesterday doesn't mean we shouldn't find out today when you show signs that make us suspicious that you are not well. So every time you behave the way you've been behaving, I will have to ask you the question, are you well, just to reassure myself that we are not subjecting you to conditions that you are not able to operate under. I'm sorry to have interrupted your question, Mr. Whiting, but I had to check if the witness is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you testified, did you not, that there was no -- nothing was accomplished at the negotiations in New York, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you went to Geneva in March and that you met with the Croat side again in April and May of 1993 but you said -- you testified, and this is at page 44 of the first day, that no agreement was reached on those occasions. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The assembly of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina was also involved in the decision making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did I understand your testimony in your direct examination correctly that there was no agreement reached until the 15th of July 1993, which you described as the Erdut Agreement? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, sir, wasn't an agreement reached on the 6th of April 1993 but the Serb side refused to endorse it? Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't fully understand. The initials I placed on one of the documents on the 6th of April in Geneva. I said the decision about that document was taken by the assembly of the RSK and this is the point clarifying the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't tell us anything about this agreement in your direct examination, did you? You're telling about this for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked of a series of or several rounds of negotiations we had during that month in Geneva. I wasn't over the three months in Geneva. I didn't really talk about it because you didn't ask me about it. If you wish me to, I will talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, no, sir, that's not right, is it? In fact on the first day of your testimony, you were asked about this time period and about agreements and you testified, and I can read it to you if you like, it's on page 44. You testified that we met again in April and May. "However no agreement was reached on either occasion." That was your testimony in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by this answer of mine today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, no agreement was reached because the Serb side refused to endorse an agreement that you had accepted during the negotiations, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't accept it. I promised Mr. Owen that we would recommend it to the assembly because we did not have the powers inherent with the assembly to accept such an agreement. Should the assembly prove to be in agreement with the paper, then the initials I placed on the agreement would signify that the RSK had accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the RSK assembly did not accept the agreement, isn't that correct? This was a cease-fire agreement. And the RSK assembly did not accept it, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RSK assembly, as a legislative body, did not accept the agreement and we informed Lord David Owen accordingly. Now, with your permission, if I can explain what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've answered the question, if I could ask my next question, which is that -- when you testified, then, in your direct examination that "the government did not reject a single proposal made by international mediators, we accepted all their proposals and negotiated with Croats," that was not true, was it? You've just now told us that the Serb side did not accept this agreement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the proposals for negotiations were accepted by us. You are misinterpreting my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So now what you're telling us is not that you accepted every proposal but that you accepted to negotiate on every occasion. Is that now your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We accepted all proposals for negotiations and we always sat down at the negotiating table.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see. If we could look at another document, and I think you'll be particularly interested in this document because you've made reference to it in your testimony, 00313329, and this is a report of the Secretary-General dated the 15th of May 1993. And this is a document that if we could look at paragraph 10, this is a document that you referred to with the reference to -- that contains the reference to Serbs being displaced from territories of Croatia. It's on page 3, paragraph 10. It says, at the bottom there, it says, "According to UNHCR figures dated 19 March 1993 the number of Serb refugees and displaced persons who have fled from Croatia to Serbia and the UNPAs approximately 251.000, now exceeds the number of Croats who were displaced from the UNPAs to Croatia." That's the reference from the Secretary-General that you were referring to in your direct examination; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me what paragraph are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's paragraph 10. It jumps from page 3 to page 4 so it's -- at the end of paragraph 10 appears at the top of the screen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's the document that you were referring to, isn't it, Mr. Jarcevic? You nodded your head but that doesn't get recorded on the transcript so you have to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document which presented a partial truth about the expulsion of Serbs by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's go back and look at paragraph 8 of this document. And this is a reference to the negotiations and the provisional agreement that we were speaking about. It says, "As regards resolution 802, representatives of the co-chairman in New York, Geneva and elsewhere have negotiated at great length with both parties to secure an agreement to implement the cease-fire and related provisions. On 6 April 1993, a provisional agreement was signed which required the endorsement of both sides. Although UNPROFOR held three lengthy meetings with the local Serb authorities to explain how it would implement the agreement operationally, and to clarify other related matters, no such endorsement had been forthcoming from the Serb side as of 10 May 1993." And that's true, isn't it, what's written there? I'm sorry, I didn't hear an answer. Is that true, sir, what's written in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. I testified a moment ago precisely along these lines. Of course, here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, you've answered the question. Let's look at paragraph 4, please, of this document. It's on page -- that's on page 2. And -- yeah, thank you. At the end of paragraph 4 it says, "During the negotiation of the peacekeeping plan, however, it was repeatedly emphasised to the local Serb leadership in what were to become the UNPAs that in practice the only basis for a settlement was their acceptance of Croatian sovereignty in return for guarantees of their minority rights. They never accepted this position or concealed their determination to press for independence from Croatia." And that's true, too, isn't it, Mr. Jarcevic? The Serb side never accepted Croatian sovereignty in return for guarantees of their minority rights.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we were never a minority in Croatia. We were a constituent nation on an equal footing with Croats, and here it never says why this was taken away from us. Who was the right to deprive the English of their sovereignty in Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could answer the question, the Serb side never accepted Croatian sovereignty in return for guarantees of their minority rights. And let's take minority here in being in numerical terms because you accept, do you not, that the Serbs were a numerical minority in Croatia in terms of population?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Croatian state killed more than a million Serbs over four years, then we found ourselves in quite a numerical minority compared to Croats but does anyone have the right to commit genocide in order to seize territory? Look at the UN charter and you will see that it says there that no one has that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that speech, sir. Now, could you please answer the question? The question is the Serb side never accepted Croatian sovereignty in exchange for guarantees of their minority rights. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't want to become a minority. This isn't a speech. These are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You could not accept that the -- the Serb side could not accept being a minority population, being a minority within the Croatian state, isn't that true? And therefore insisted again and again and again until the very end for its own state. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What Croatia took away from them on the 25th of December 1995 -- sorry, 1990, by amending its constitution. It was an illegal, unlawful change to the constitution because it shouldn't have been amended without the participation and consent of the Serbs in the assembly. The Serbs representing a state forming nation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 866, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, since you were the Foreign Minister in February of 1993, you certainly must have been aware that Veljko Dzakula negotiated what was called the Daruvar agreement with the Croatian government, and the agreement was an agreement that by peaceful means and dialogue, existing problems, certainly in Western Slavonia, would be resolved including utilities problems, water, electricity, roads, contacts between families. You're aware of that Daruvar agreement, aren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're aware also, aren't you, that as a result of negotiating that agreement, Mr. Dzakula was suspended from his position as Deputy Prime Minister in the RSK government and later in the fall of 1993 he was arrested and detained by that government. You know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there is a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. The reason for that was that he had made agreement with the Croatian side, isn't that the reason, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not conclude agreement with the Croat side and you another got to mention that he was a minister in the cabinet of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I think I did mention that. And he -- he reached a -- the Daruvar agreement with the Croatian side and that is why he was suspended from his position of minister in the cabinet, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because he did not have authorisation to negotiate independently. What he did, he did as a private person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what authorisation you had to negotiate when you were sent to -- you say you were sent to London in June of 1994 by Milan Martic and you were no longer Foreign Minister, you were just an adviser to the president, but yet you went to London to negotiate. Did you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only the Foreign Minister who goes to attend negotiations. Remember, Averell Harriman from the history books.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The point is that when you did that, when you went to London, you were not -- you were not dismissed from your position as an adviser. You were not arrested and detained, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the head of state and the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina approved my travel. Nobody approved anything for Mr. Dzakula. We didn't even know that he was going to negotiate and it is important for the Trial Chamber to know that Croats had promised him secret negotiations and then, by chance, they published it in all the media. They wanted thus to create a rift in the government of the Serbian Krajina and that's what they achieved. It was not enough for them that in the area about which Dzakula negotiated, there was not a single settlement left standing. 130 villages were destroyed together with all the infrastructures, and the Croats used the area to dump radioactive material and waste there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that the only reason that Mr. Dzakula lost his position and was later arrested and detained was because he was unauthorised to conduct these negotiations, not because he dared to reach agreement with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the British government would replace each and every minister who would go anywhere to negotiate without prior approval of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about the Erdut agreement which you testified about, and you described the agreement -- this was the agreement that was reached on the 15th of July 1993. You described it in your testimony as follows: This is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, what are you saying no to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter said January and was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was evidently a misinterpretation because I said July so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the record says July also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, but no doubt in B/C/S he -- it must have been misinterpreted by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's July 15th, 1993, the Erdut agreement, right? You've nodded your head.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described it in your testimony as follows: There is at page 46 and 47 of the transcript of the first day of your testimony. "The contents of the agreement was as follows. Its main feature was that after the agreement was signed, both governments would settle up commissions for cooperation in all areas. Those commissions were supposed to bring both sides to a state of two cantons like the one that would begin to exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Dayton Accords. But first the commissions were to work on reuniting transport, trade, economy, culture, education, et cetera." Now, isn't it true, sir, that the Erdut agreement had nothing to do with setting up cantons or reuniting or commissions to reunite on transport or trade? It was strictly an agreement involving the movement and withdrawal of armed forces in certain areas along the confrontation line? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. And representatives of the two superpowers would never have come to Erdut for such a trifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, why don't we look at the agreement. It's 01749241. And if you could just scroll down, please. This version of the agreement is signed just by one side but -- if necessary, I have one that's signed by both sides. Here, that -- is that your signature, sir, S Jarcevic, 15th of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could look at the agreement, in paragraph 1, it says no Croatian armed forces or police in the areas specified on the attached map, paragraph 2, talks about UNPROFOR. Paragraph 3, talks about who will be present in certain villages. Paragraph 4 withdrawal of Croatian armed forces and police from certain areas. And then paragraph 5, is the only paragraph that even remotely approaches anything like what you talked about. It says "Both sides agree to intensify their efforts to reach a negotiated solution to all problems existing between them starting with a cease-fire agreement to be negotiated by UNPROFOR." That's the Erdut agreement, isn't it, sir? It has nothing to do with cantons or commissions to resolve trade or commerce or anything. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that item 5 is related to all that I have said. I didn't say that the term canton was written anywhere, but the purpose of the agreement was to bring about that situation in practice, that Krajina and Croatia should be united in a way that was later implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We discussed that with representatives of the United States and Russia. You miss represented this agreement, though. You said that it is solely about borders and the deployment of forces. Please, this was supposed to remove the consequences of the Croatian aggression of the 22nd of January 1993. You see how large an area was occupied, the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I submit to you and I put to you that I did not misrepresent the agreement. You did in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir, because commissions were supposed to work and they did start to work. They were ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the commissions that you are referring to were strictly to enforce this agreement, this cease-fire agreement. They had nothing to do with creating cantons or anything like that. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that international representatives were hoping that one single state would emerge with two cantons, with two state forming nations like it was before 1991. That was done in verbal discussion. It was not reflected in the text. I said yesterday that this was just a framework paper, a framework agreement. I said that before and I'm repeating it now, Mr. Whiting. And may I just add nothing thing? There is a report --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir I think you've answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 867, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I'd like to look at an interview with Goran Hadzic shortly after the Erdut agreement. This is R 0330574. No? It's not? It has a -- it should have that number and then redacted at the end, RED, because the top part is redacted. You have it? Okay. We have a hard copy if it can't be pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there is some difficulty with the e-court if we could just put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- it's an interview dated the 24th to the 25th of July 1993 in Belgrade Borba with Goran Hadzic. And I'd like to look, please, at the second page of the document. And about halfway down the page, it says, "The aim is for us to create a Serbian state, and this already exists and is even partially recognised because you see the Croats are now talking to us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on the screen, it's about halfway down. Though it's on the -- on the document it's actually about a quarter of the way down. I don't know if the usher can see where it is. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What Mr. Hadzic said there is true, isn't it, that the aim was to create a Serbian state, right, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I will answer with just a small addition. Yes, and it was confirmed by 28 MPs of the Council of Europe several months ago, including a MP in the lower house of the British parliament. It was said that Croatia had to be set up as a two-nation state and so on and so forth. So Goran Hadzic was pursuing the interests of the Serb people based on their ethnic and historic rights. I believe that the Republic of Serbian Krajina has to be restored as a state, be it within the framework of Croatia as until 1990 or independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I think you fully answered that question after the word yes. So I'd ask you again, please to focus?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And answer as briefly as possible. Now, a little further down, it says, "Before --" and I don't know if this is on the screen here. Okay. It's at the bottom of the screen. It says, "Before the beginning of the armed struggle, I thought we would achieve our aims without calling the people to arms but when I saw that this was not possible, we embarked on a military struggle which we won." And that's true also, isn't it, sir? That the Serb side embarked on a military struggle to achieve its aims of a Serbian state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to defend itself and create its state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the registrar to help on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it on e-court now? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just had to find my place here. If we could scroll down a little bit, please, there we go. And at the bottom there, if you see it says, "As for the Serbs who have remained in Croatia," if we could focus in on the sort of 10, 15 sentences after that. Right there where the arrow, perfect. Now if we could zoom in on those sentences after that. Or maybe that's not possible. Yeah. There we go. Yeah, okay. It says, "As for the Serbs who remained -- this is what Mr. Hadzic is saying, as for the Serbs who have remained in Croatia these are Serbs or rather the former leadership of the communist party of which there are very few. The other Serbs who live in Croatia are Serbian fascists who support Tudjman. They are loyal to his authority and it is best that they remain there. An example of the former is Dusan Dragosevic [phoen] and of the latter is Milan Djukic. There are a total of 50.000 such Serbs in Croatia. We do not need to cooperate with such so-called Serbs." This reflects the attitude of the RSK leadership towards Serbs who remained in Croatia, does it not, that they were essentially traitors to the Serb cause, isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely correct. 400.000 Serbs were expelled. I say that once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you agree with what I said in my question, which is that Serbs who remained in Croatia were considered by the RSK leadership to be traitors to the Serb cause?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber I would like to explain why Mr. Hadzic mentioned communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you first answer my question? You agree that the attitude of the RSK leadership is that Serbs who remained in Croatia were traitors to the Serb cause?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were open traitors and that's whom Mr. Hadzic meant. I had the same opinion about traitors and I believe you do too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you please not to speculate on what I believe. Just answer my questions. Now, I want you to look at one other passage from this article and it's about something we were talking about earlier. And I just need to find the place. Okay. It's on the screen. Mr. Hadzic is asked this question -- I'm sorry, sir, what is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpreter very well any more. I don't know what happened with my reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for telling us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's excellent now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic is asked this question: You have broken with some close associates, why? And the answer he gives was, the difference was obvious. For example with some Serbs from Western Slavonia, an example is Veljko Dzakula who sometimes secretly negotiates with the Croats. He was in the government but our concepts of the struggle were different from the beginning. He and his supporters are no longer any kind of political force. They wanted to go for cohabitation with the Croats and we wanted to be neighbours only. When it comes to Zdravko Zivkovic [phoen] a former government member, he is an honest Serb but at one point he could not find a solution. For us, cohabitation with the Croats is treachery. We will never agree to this even if a new war begins. Does this accurately reflect the attitude of the RSK leadership towards Mr. Dzakula's positions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we know what coexistence in Croatia is, then it's clearly yes. This coexistence implies expulsion of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally I want to look at one more quote from this, and if we could just scroll down just a little bit on the text, there, just a tiny bit more, there. Finally he says, Mr. Lajic says, "Our aim is well known and there is a unified Serbian state regardless of where its capital will be. I want to move freely around the Serbian lands." Now, that's a reference to all of the Serbian lands in the former Yugoslavia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was our platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 868, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to turn to 1994, please. You testified about the Zagreb agreement that was reached in March of 1994. Isn't it true that after that agreement was reached, the Serb side obstructed and delayed at every opportunity in negotiating the economic agreement which was finally concluded in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Krajina did not obstruct a single agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, it took so long to achieve the economic agreement that the political agreement which was later referred to as the Z-4 plan was accelerated because the economic agreement was taking so long, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are not talking about the structure of negotiations If we were I could tell you where Croats were not right, where Serbs were not right. They all probably had their positions, that depended on circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But the point is, isn't it, that the Serb side delayed and obstructed the negotiations concerning the economic agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, one of the reasons was that resolution 815, if I'm not mistaken banned the vehicles in Republika Srpska from moving about. We had asked the Security Council to remove that particular provision which was never done and that was the reason for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about the Z-4 plan. You constantly referred to the fact that it was an insult because it covered only two districts, which you said included 11 municipalities. In fact, it covered nearly the entire territory of sectors north and south, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that it covered all the territories in sectors north and south where the Serbs were a majority before 1991? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only 11 municipalities, sir. List them all and you'll see which ones are left out. Most of the Krajina population lived in the Western Slavonia which was practically cleansed, in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. These areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. First of all do you know how many municipalities were included in sectors north and south?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All in all, Krajina had 28 municipalities, but the municipalities mentioned in Z-4 are not these RSK municipalities, but the municipalities in Croatia which were much smaller than was customary in Yugoslavia. Some local communes were even transformed into municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back -- because perhaps talking about municipalities is confusing, let's go back to my original question. The Z-4 plan would have applied to all of the territory within sectors north and south where Serbs were a majority before 1991. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, that's not true. Were it true, then the Z-4 would have mentioned north and south, and that wasn't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have Exhibit 381 in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 381 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is the Z-4 plan, and if we could go to page 5, please, of the document -- I'm sorry, that's page 3. It might be page 5 on the e-court but -- now, at the very beginning of the agreement, it talks about where this -- what area is contained, and if we could scroll down it says, it talks about boundaries, it says, there shall be an established the autonomous Serbian Krajina to consist of the territory indicated on map one in annex A, and then there is a footnote and if we could go back down to the bottom, it describes the territory. It says this territory will be a single, continuous territory comprising the Serb majority areas the United Nations protected areas sectors north and south as defined in the 1991 census with due consideration to geographic and economic factors. So, in fact, the agreement applied, as I stated, to sector -- those areas of sectors north and south where the Serbs were a majority in the 1991 census. Do you accept that now, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says clearly here within the area sectors north and south, within them, not all the entire sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you claimed in your testimony that Milan Martic rejected this agreement because the UNPROFOR mandate had not been extended. But in fact, isn't it true that he rejected it for the same reason that you say this is insulting because it did not give statehood and it only gave autonomy? Isn't that really the reason that Milan Martic rejected it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the real reason, counsel. Apologies?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor misinterpreted the witness's evidence. The witness spoke of the fact that Mr. Martic did not take into consideration the plan because he asked Ambassador Galbraith to first solve the status of UNPROFOR. Therefore, it wasn't that he rejected the plan, as the witness's evidence was presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can put the question slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the reason he refused even to accept the plan, to take a copy of it from the international negotiators, is that -- and I'm going to give two reasons now: Number one, that the plan did not offer statehood; and secondly because Mr. Milosevic told him to reject it? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter remark you make was widely exploited in the media, namely that it was Milosevic who ordered the RSK president to reject it. I don't know anything about that and Mr. Martic had never told me that something of the sort happened. I told you that I was in Belgrade at the time the plan was taken to Knin and I said that the main reason was that there were hints along the lines that the RSK would no longer be a United Nations protected area. This was what caused concern with the president, and he wanted to appeal to Ambassador Galbraith to use his offices not to have the status of the international forces in Krajina changed but there wasn't a single body that would accept the plan that had been offered for four times. Why was its name changed? Why was it that the US authority was used to try and push this agreement through four or five times? It's as if these international factors were playing funny games or having fun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, isn't it true that the Z-4 plan offered to the Serbs in Croatia a degree of autonomy that went far beyond anything that had been offered before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't offer that. You could have offered a four storey building in Croatia but this didn't apply to the entire Serb population. I even wonder at you putting this question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're confusing two issues, I would submit. I -- I am not talking about the area applied to. What I'm talking about is the degree of autonomy that was offered and you would accept, would you not, that that went far beyond anything that had been offered before. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't commend this as a good offer if it applies to 60.000 people and there were about 1 million Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've not answered my question, sir. Please listen to my question and answer my question. My question is: The degree of autonomy that was offered in the agreement went far beyond anything that had been offered to the Serb side before; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side wasn't offered anything from the Croat side. This was not operational, as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I put the question to you now three or four times and I would submit you've refused to answer it and the Trial Chamber will have to draw its own conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will take a short adjournment and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Whiting, there is an urgent housekeeping matter that needs to be attended to, and for that purpose, may we please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, in your direct examination, you claimed that Mr. Martic -- with respect to the renewing of UNPROFOR in 1995, you said that Mr. Martic did not get what he wanted because when UNPROFOR was renewed, it was no longer a protection force and this is -- I'll quote the transcript from page 76 to 77. You said, "Mr. Milovancevic, I think you made a slip. Mr. Martic's request had not been granted. The forces were given a different role. They were no longer a protection force." You recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's false, isn't it, sir? In fact, the protection force was given a different name. It was called UNCRO but it continued to have the role of -- the same role that it had had before with respect to protecting not just the Serbs but all communities. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It was obvious that it didn't protect because the Serbs from Krajina were expelled and the Croatian officials were happy about this. They said there is a protection area no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question and answer my question. When UNPROFOR, the mandate was renewed in March of 1995 and a new name was given to it, it had the same task with respect to protecting the communities as it had had before. That did not change. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, the -- it was changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the text of the resolution. This is 04247568. This is resolution 981, dated 31 March 1995. And this is the resolution which extended the mandate of UNPROFOR and gave it a new name called UNCRO. And if we could look at the third page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Whiting? I have a problem with my headphone. When you are speaking there are people talking over my head here. It only becomes clear when there is interpretation. I have no problem when the witness is speaking. It's when you speak that people talk over my head and I have a problem trying to disregard them to had hear what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll try again and see what happens because I think they are trying to fix it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think maybe it's hearing the interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Somehow that's being picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. It is the interpretation into B/C/S that I hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think the interpreters are trying to say something to us in the middle booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I believe you are picking it up through the microphone of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We are picking it up through the microphone of the witness. I do notice in my case that it's connected to the middle booth. Whenever the lady on the right seems to be speaking then I can normally hear that background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in we could zoom in on paragraph 5 of this resolution, paragraph 5 says that -- decides that "UNCRO shall be an interim arrangement to create the conditions that will facilitate a negotiated settlement consistent with the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia" - and here is the important part - "and which guarantees the security and rights of all communities living in a particular area of the Republic of Croatia irrespective of whether they constitute in this area a majority or a minority." So that -- they -- that was no change from before, was it? The UNCRO would continue to guarantee protection for all communities in the region; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that's not right. This does not reflect the situation at all. If you recall, the Vance Plan guaranteed all the parties that a political settlement would not be prejudiced, and item 5 which you've just read out prejudges that precisely and shows that there was reason for us to be dissatisfied. If our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because you're focusing on something different than what I'm asking you about. I'm not asking you about that. You testified in your examination-in-chief that when the mandate was extended, it was no longer a protection force. Now, you would agree, would you not, that now that you see the mandate, the extension of the mandate, here, in paragraph 5, it is in fact a protection force. Isn't that correct? It states it right there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. That's not what is written. It's written that the Republic of Serbian Krajina is Croatia, which means both the army and the police are able to enter. Para 5 gives them the right to. Whereas in the Vance Plan that was formulated in a completely different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the -- the fact that the United Nations recognised the territorial integrity of Croatia, that had in fact occurred several years before. That's nothing new. That had occurred back in -- as early as 1993. Isn't that true? That's not new to this resolution.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we always notified the Security Council that we do not accept those provisions contained in their resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that cannot -- since that was in existence for several years, the United Nations had been saying that for several years, that cannot be a reason why Mr. Martic was refusing to engage in the Z-4 process and that's not what you said in your direct examination. What you said in your direct examination is that it was no longer a protection force. Will you accept, having read paragraph 5 of the resolution, that in fact it was a protection force and the same -- it had the same role as it had had before in that regard? Will you accept that or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that because it's not written anywhere that they are a protection force. Could you read it for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "Which guarantees the security and rights of all communities living in a particular area of the Republic of Croatia irrespective of whether they constitute in this area a majority or a minority.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan was signed by the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It is not a -- it does not appear in para 5. Why was it deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence and given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will become Exhibit 869.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you agree, do you not, that after this resolution was passed on the 31st of March 1995, Mr. Martic never made any attempt whatsoever to engage the international negotiators in the Z-4 process, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. Mr. Martic, as president of the state, did indeed participate in negotiations at the proposal of the new officials who were no longer part of the protection force but part of UNCRO and you know what transpired, but Croatia reneged on everything, even the opening of the motor way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's a different subject, sir. What I'm talking about is the Z-4 process. Mr. Martic -- after the 31st of March, 1995, Mr. Martic never picked up the phone to call any of the negotiators, any of the representatives of the Z-4 process, did he? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Z-4 was never on the agenda again but you know that we first rejected it in 1992. You are reminding me of what happened three years previously, and now I'll remind you, it was humiliated both on the part of Croatia and on the part of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, again, I'll suggest that you fully answered the question after you said the Z-4 was never on the agenda again. I'm going to move on to another topic now. You testified about information that you had received about what happened in the Posavina corridor in 1992 and you testified about the death of some babies that had occurred there. When, to your information, about that occur? When in 1992, what month, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened before I became minister. I really cannot recall the month and it's quite natural that one does not keep track of various dates, including in state affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the embargo that applied to Bosnia and Herzegovina territories did not apply to humanitarian aid or medical aid, isn't that true, the embargo that was imposed by UN resolution 757 on the 30th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The embargo applied to traffic, whereas oxygen was only able to arrive by some means of transportation, certainly not by radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. It did not apply to humanitarian aid and medical supplies, true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was formally true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the ban on flights, the no-flight -- the ban on flights which was imposed on the 9th of October 1992, so well after these events that you have described, also did not apply to humanitarian flights, isn't that true? This was a ban that was imposed by resolution 781 on the 9th of October 1992. You agree that it did not apply to humanitarian flights, true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's formally true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified about incursions that occurred in the Medak pocket, Maslenica bridge, Miljevac plateau. Those territories were all largely within the -- what were known as the pink zones, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the pink zones were territories that were supposed to revert to Croatian control, isn't that true? They were the first territories that were supposed to, under the UN plan, they were supposed to revert to Croatian control, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the Serb people gained confidence in the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was a condition imposed by the Serb side, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's written in a document of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, the Serb side, the representatives from the RSK, consistently and constantly impeded the return of the pink zone territories to Croatian control, isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Mr. Thornberry who was in charge always kept telling us there is still no confidence in the Croatian authorities because they kept crossing the border and killing civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified in your direct examination that you remained the assistant for foreign affairs to President Martic until the 26th of February 1996. Does that mean that Mr. Martic considered himself the president of the RSK until that date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The current government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina treats him as their president.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say the current government, you're referring to the government that exists in exile, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government in exile that has opened its representative office in Paris under the decision of the Foreign Minister of France.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you a member of that government in exile?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am just an adviser of that government in exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Mr. Martic continues to be the president of that government in exile, even to this day?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he will until we are able to hold new elections for the president of Republic of Serbian Krajina, and he may win those elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have -- continue to have contact with Mr. Martic after the 26th of February 1996?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are on friendly terms. However, the government of Yugoslavia banned the representatives and authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from working, from operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I will ask you a couple of questions that emanate from the cross-examination. One of the first points put to you by the Prosecutor yesterday was your letter to Aleksa Buha. As far as I remember the date was the 11th of September 1993. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do. We saw it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see that letter again on the monitor? It's Exhibit 861. Before it appears on our screens, can you explain to us what was the reason why you wrote that letter? What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under the circumstances when the Croatian authorities were shooting an and violating the cease-fire on our borders whereas leaders in Republika Srpska meaning Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina had quarrelled amongst themselves, and the media were writing only about those quarrels in Banja Luka and in Pale and nobody paid any attention to the danger coming from the Croatian side against the Republic of Serbian Krajina and I was begging them in that letter to stop fighting amongst themselves, that we were facing a grave danger, expecting an offensive from Croatia and that all Serbs should help defend those borders there because I said yesterday, and allow me to explain it, that schooling and education in Croatia was directed precisely at fostering hatred towards Serbs. In Croatian textbooks, in addition to the sentence I quoted, said Serbs should be killed with an ax. I had to say that this was producing criminals and it does. It's like including Hitler's ideas in German textbooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jarcevic. Do you remember which date the operation Medak pocket took place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was on the 8th of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This letter you wrote is dated the 11th September, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's why I wrote it because attention needed to be paid to strategic matters to the fate of the people and the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Look at the very beginning of that text, which is right in front of you. The first sentence after the introduction distinguished Mr. Buha reads, "The Croatian army has attacked all points of our border." What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were skirmishes in other locations in order to divert attention from the main strike in Lika where 11 Serb villages were raised to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a little down below, three sentences below, you say, "I'm writing this to you so that you could say to officers and soldiers in Banja Luka that the Serbian people is facing possible defeat." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this sentence, can one draw the conclusion that you are making an appeal and pointing to what was going on; rather, I'll rephrase my question to avoid objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the -- I think Mr. Milovancevic anticipated my objection which is that it was leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The appropriate question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have already answered in part. Was the political situation in Bosnia the reason why you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're still leading, Mr. Milovancevic. This witness is your witness. Ask him why he wrote the letter. He will tell you. Don't suggest to him why he wrote the letter. You're not cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, the letter is dated 11 September 1993. Why did you write this to Mr. Buha?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was three days after a horrible massacre in the Serbian Krajina. That is the third day into the massacre. With something like that going on, how could they be quarrelling about dividing positions or offices, ranks, in Banja Luka? I proceeded from the assumption that every Serb should be engaged to defend every yard of Serbian ground. In this case, two Serbian states west of Drina had to have the same policy. That was my appeal. And that's the oath that our heads of state and the parliaments of both governments had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Prosecutor asked you, when you were invoking the Second World War in this letter, or rather, in the answers you gave to the Prosecutor concerning the Second World War, were you appealing to Serbs to be afraid of Croats? This letter that you wrote, did it have that meaning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of that letter was that Serbs should be afraid of the Croatian state. I was never in favour of condemning a whole nation for the evil committed by their state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please don't suggest answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an independent person. Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take care, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, when I'm talking to counsel, it is not for you to comment. I've never commented on your independence or the lack of it. Just don't answer me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. I will obey from now on. I did break the rule once. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, yesterday and today, our learned friend from the Prosecution showed you several documents of the United Nations, reports by the Secretary-General and resolutions. What are those documents in terms of their contents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: There are documents which may be legal, social or rather sociological, economic, or political in nature. In which category would you place these documents of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say they are political documents because they do not represent a single state, they represent -- or they are on behalf of the international community. However, the Croatian platform and the Croatian propaganda was full of quotations from these texts and I repeat to you what General Nambiar said to me: Croatian crimes and evils against Serbs are no where written about. That was sealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the Prosecutor put to you a report by General Nambiar yesterday where his position on the militia or the police of the Serbian Krajina is expressed or rather the weapons they carried. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that letter was dated sometime in end July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date but I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please see this document on our screens? It's a letter written to Mr. Goulding on behalf of the UNPROFOR and General Nambiar in particular. Let me just find the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 574.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Did I hear you correctly, 574? The Registry heard the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This letter shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday, is it from General Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th, and after that it's not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It should be July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the time of the Miljevacki plateau?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a month before July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, were the troops in the UNPA, the international troops?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were a protection force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was General Nambiar the force commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say several times during your testimony that Croatian forces on that occasion travestied the agreement and killed 40 per cents [as interpreted] of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the offices of General Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. It's either a leading question or it's asked and answered. If he's just repeating what he said in his testimony it's on the transcript there is no need to ask it again but I would suggest it's also just a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was really trying, Your Honour, to keep this as short as possible and maybe I broke a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You ask your own witness leading questions and if you're asking him something that he has already talked about, there is no need for you to ask that question because it's already on the transcript. Now, please try not to ask leading questions. The objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, what was the position of General Nambiar on the long barrels carried by the Krajina Police that he mentions in this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and all his successors constantly raised the issue because it was part of the Vance Plan, and when we asked those gentlemen about other clauses of the Vance Plan, they never had anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During the activities of the Croatian army on the Miljevac plateau, did the UNPROFOR play its role as defined in the Vance Plan and that is to protect all the population from armed attack?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not in the least. I don't think anything was done against Croatia because sometimes it even happened that UN troops were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, you spoke about the Maslenica operation. Can you remind us of the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22nd January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was General Nambiar still the force commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think he had gone back to India by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the UNPROFOR in that area where aggression occurred?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And their number was not reduced and most of them were precisely in Dalmatia where the Croatian army struck. It was also the Kenyan Battalion that was there and I believe several Kenyan soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Even after such operations of the Croatian army, was it still demanded from the Serb side to take long barrels away from their police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That demand was constantly made. It continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we see on our screens another document, a report of the general secretary, 24600? Exhibit 75. Do you remember that in connection with these reports of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, my colleague from the Prosecution asked you yesterday inter alia about the situation on the ground in view of the special police and the fact that they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When he put this document to you, that is now in front of us, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What follows is the report of the UN Secretary-General. Can we just see the date, 28th September 1992. Regarding this document, the Prosecutor put to you paragraph 34, that indicates that violations of the Vance Plan, and this is the substance of the paragraph, led to a state close to anarchy in which ethnic cleansing was committed and this was all -- this violation was practically the Serb police. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we look at paragraph 3 of this report, S 24/600. This paragraph 3 is in chapter 1. It's entitled, "Violations of the cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have subparagraphs A, B, C and D, and that's an enumeration of the major incidents that create tensions in that area, and it reads, in subparagraph A, on 7th August, 1992, fighting erupted in an area adjacent to the southeastern portion of Sector West. Apparently due to attempts by armed elements from the Croatian side to cross the Sava River and attack Bosnian Serb elements south of the river. It goes on to describe that heavy weaponry was used and nine dead bodies were left lined. Do you see this?
