utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In subpara B, do you see where it reads that on the 13th of August 1992, a group of Serbs, villagers in Sector East, were attempting to harvest maize. On that occasion they were attacked by the Croatian army, four were killed, and 19 taken prisoners, or hostages. Does it say so here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the 700 incursions across the border of Serbian Krajina that I've been talking about for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In C we see that on the 21st of August three Serbs so-called border militia personnel were shot dead in the vicinity of the confrontation line in Sector East and in D it says that in the last week in August a large group tried to infiltrate through Sector North into the Bihac/Cazin area. It was intercepted by the local Serb police and the UNPROFOR established they had been mobilised and trained by the Croatian army in certain areas in Croatia, and they had been infiltrated in small groups into Bosnia and Herzegovina to join fighting there. This was raised with President Tudjman on the 31st of August, 1992, by undersecretary Marek Goulding and President Tudjman promised it would never happen again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those Croats went to assist one of the warring Bosnian groups. There were two such groups that we discussed the already and one of them had been expelled or exiled into the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at paragraph 8? It says on the 4th of September, undersecretary Goulding, Marrack Goulding, reached agreement with Serb authorities about demobilisation of those forces in two stages, the first to start on the 11th September, another one later on the 20th September or rather the second one was to start on the 15th of October. Now, could the counsel read more slowly, please? I'd like to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreters are asking that you read a little more slowly and we also realise that you probably have a hard copy of the document before we get it on the screen you're already reading paragraph 8 and you left us all behind. Quite apart from reading slowly you just -- your pace of dealing with the issues is just too fast. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this warning, Your Honour. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see paragraph 8 on the screen, which speaks of the agreement with Marrack Goulding with these police forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time this report was written, which was the 28th of September 1992, you were still not a minister?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You came in later on and you were able to familiarise yourself with the situation from government documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also covered by the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the conclusions based on a document thus presented corresponded to the situation on the ground or even to what was contained in other documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, once such crimes are recorded in a document, Security Council organs do not take any actions against Croatia and Croatia could carry out 700 more such attacks without any repercussions whereas the Serbs were always the ones to be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, thanks once again for the speech. Please answer the question that was put to you now. Do you believe that the conclusions based on a document thus presented correspond to the situation and the ground or even to what was contained in other documents? That was the question put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The events happened this way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I asked you whether the conclusions could the effect that the Serbs and the special police were responsible for such a situation on the ground, do they correspond to the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to explain this and I'm sorry that it was interpreted as a speech. I don't think I need to repeat what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat what you said, Mr. Jarcevic, because, indeed, it was a speech. A simple answer to that question is "yes, I believe" or "no, I don't believe," or "no, I have no opinion on the matter."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, both in the course of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, it was mentioned that you, as the Foreign Minister of the RSK, had an office in Belgrade. Can you tell us where your office premises were located and who they were owned by?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the very centre of town and I believe or rather I'm sure that they belonged to the municipality of Belgrade. The address was Terazija, number 3, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jarcevic. Perhaps I wasn't precise enough. You gave us the location of these premises. I wanted to know whether these office premises were someone's ownership, whether you rented them out, who rented them out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were rented out by the government of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this in fact then a representation office of the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly that, yes, but the representation office was in an adjacent street, Mosa Pijade number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the document entitled, "Erdut agreement," my learned friend from the Prosecution showed you the text of the agreement today dated 15 July 1993. Do you recall that it was a brief text containing, I believe, five paragraphs? You were commenting on it and the document bears your signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to explain something concerning article 4 but the Prosecutor told me that I did not need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at Exhibit 867, which is the text of the Erdut Agreement? Is this the text we talked a moment ago about, Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to add the following, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 4, the main motor way was supposed to be open for traffic, and I said that the commissions should discuss other branches of the economy in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In presenting this document to you, the Prosecutor said that this document concerned a cease-fire agreement and some technical matters. I'd like to know the following: Did Mr. Tudjman accept this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he rejected it publicly stating that this was out of force, null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't think this arises out of my questions. My questions were the content of the agreement. I did not go into whether Mr. Tudjman had accepted it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Does that arise out of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to know who the signatory tri of the Croatian side on the Croatian side was because Mr. Jarcevic signed the document, and the Prosecutor asked him whether he had accepted the document on behalf of the Serb side. Mr. Jarcevic answered in the affirmative. I only wanted to inquire about the Croat side. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that arise out of the cross-examination, Mr. Milovancevic? If I remember well, Mr. Whiting indicated that there is a version that is signed by both parties, if that is required, but that's about all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wanted to put a brief question to Mr. Jarcevic as to the fate of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that but does that arise out of cross examination? The purpose of re-examination is to clarify issues that came out during cross-examination, that are not clear. The cross-examination related to the content of this agreement. The question is, does -- is your question as a result of the cross-examination? Are you challenging the authenticity of the document because it's not signed by the opposite side, which was not the issue also during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will withdraw this question. The witness gave his answer during the examination-in-chief and I will not insist on it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact, if you had got the answer during examination-in-chief, then there is no point in raising it again in re-examination. You just are burdening the record unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, the Prosecutor presented you with a portion of the interview by Mr. Hadzic, the president of the RSK. He showed you a text where Mr. Hadzic states that -- or as he says, our objective is to unify, to unite into a Serbian state, regardless of where the capital is. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our main goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Jarcevic, the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Yugoslavia, did they ever accept this goal of yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, kept rejecting our plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Jarcevic, I have one question concerning your function, your work as a minister in Belgrade, with your office in Belgrade. You explained to us that within the technical and other assistance to other countries, and especially to the RSK, Yugoslavia also paid you and the offices of your ministry. Therefore, you said, there were particularly close contacts with Yugoslavia maintained, and you explained yesterday you used to listen to their opinion, and on the other hand you mentioned an occasion where you were not completely informed by them but there was apparently a close communication. And so my question would be how did you maintain this communication? Who was forwarding -- who was communicating to whom? Was this in a diplomatic way or in a direct way, with you personally? In other words, did you have a ambassador who conveyed information to you, or -- and if yes, who was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you how this was done from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. All the documents coming out of the foreign ministry, a copy of them was forwarded to the foreign ministry of Yugoslavia to the foreign ministry of Republika Srpska and often times to the Montenegrin government in -- at Podgorica. The communication between the RSK foreign ministry and these offices was irregular or did not happen regularly. A moment ago when I answered the question as to whether Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, were supporting our idea of forming a unified Serb state, I said no. This was the strategic orientation of Serbia and Yugoslavia. I can confirm this by telling you that the assembly of Yugoslavia in 1991 rejected the proposal for the unification of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. This was a great disappointment to us. We were unable to understand this. But we adapted ourselves to the situation. We maintained such relations with Yugoslavia as were possible and as were allowed by Yugoslavia. For instance, I asked the federal government of Yugoslavia and the foreign ministry of Yugoslavia to place at our disposal the Yugoslav diplomacy world wide in order for us to distribute our documents and which would collect information for us and contact the United Nations agencies on our behalf. This was rejected by the Yugoslav foreign ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Were you telling me examples of communication but my real question was how this communication was working and do I understand you correctly that this was in direct way, it was not on a diplomatic way, there was no embassy to Yugoslavia or an embassy -- a Yugoslavian ambassador to -- or whose jurisdiction covered the RSK and who then conveyed this. This was a direct -- was such a close communication that it was directly being done, like a person from the ministry of Yugoslavia would call you on the telephone directly, for example? Did that happen regularly? Or write a letter to you? Or meet you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This did not happen regularly. There was no customary practice. I said yesterday and today that we would receive some documents accidentally because some of their ministry officials would realise that we needed to have them. Even some of the resolutions that the Prosecutor was presenting me with, we did not receive directly. Some we did. But some reached us with a delay. We wanted to open our embassies in Serbia and Montenegro but both governments refused to do that. We even published that information in the papers. We meant it as a joke but it was not well received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have diplomatic relations with other countries outside the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to have diplomatic relations with us. In some letters, we were addressed as the foreign ministry, as a state, but that was only the representation office of Japan and Nigeria. I believe you will receive these documents. In their communication with us, they addressed us properly as the foreign Ministry of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. When responding to any proposals we put forth or any such communication. The only official recognition that we received was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat from whom he -- they received recognition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was kind of recognition we never had from Yugoslavia or Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you please repeat from whom did you receive -- could you please repeat from whom you received recognition?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we had a mutual recognition with a small republic that is to be found between Ukraine and Moldova which came into being with the dissolution of the U.S.S.R. Secondly, the Japanese and Nigerian embassies sent memos to us in the form that they sent to other countries with our full title and without inverted commas. Other embassies, if you want to know, normally sent over their own people and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You can finish this sentence, please, but then could you add what republic between Ukraine and was it between Ukraine and Moldova.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moldova. Pridnestrovaskai republic. Transdniestria republic. We call it Pridnestrovaskai republic and it exist today. However, if you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Did you want to add something in your last sentence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have been negotiating with some other governments in exile, possible mutual recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fine. That was my question. I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You had been asked in examination-in-chief about the circumstances under which you came to be a minister in 1992, I believe, and you said you heard about a planned massacre in Bosnia and Herzegovina of Serbs. How did you learn of this planned massacre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you who the man was who brought it over to Belgrade to us but I can tell you that it was a colonel, Stanislav Nikic, my fellow countryman who obtained the information, urgently placed a call to me, and I in turn called the Portuguese Ambassador to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you also spoke about the number of Serbs who had been expelled and you said that Germany was the only country that allowed Serb refugees to go to Germany. How many Serb refugees were there in Germany, to your knowledge, can you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that is not precisely the way I put it. There were refugees in all countries but the government of the Federal Republic of Germany publicly -- made a public statement about the refugees and said that they would be returned to Croatia. We in turn informed Germany that these people were deprived of their collective citizenship which had not been recorded in history ever and that if they are sent back to Croatia, they would be expelled just as they were the first time. We also informed them that their private properties and flats were confiscated. Germany did not respond to us officially but it was a Mr. Ahrends who told us and gave us assurance that is these people would not be sent back to Croatia. Germany did not want to take up so many people. It was Austria, Australia, Canada, Great Britain, France, all these countries received refugees, so what we know is that there was the total of 251.000 people who left but some of them also left for Yugoslavia, and for the Republika Srpska. Yet Ahrends complained about the fact that the Germany was bearing the brunt of the financial burden stemming from the refugees coming from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's really numbers that I had wanted to get from you. And one final question: You were asked by counsel, Mr. Milovancevic, if either yourself or Milan Martic did anything in any way to obstruct the return of displaced Croats to the RSK. Now you only answered in respect of yourself but you didn't give an answer in respect of Mr. Milan Martic. So could you now answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the head of state, Mr. Martic -- our position was as follows: If that is placed on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we are dealing with Mr. Martic's response and did he do anything to obstruct the return of displaced Croats to the territory of RSK? You've already answered. This is what I wanted to stress to you. Learned counsel sell was trying to get it from you on the record, you answered in respect of yourself. Deal specifically with Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic shared my position, which was that Serbs and Croats should be allowed to return, and that the policy should not be that only care should be taken of Croats and their return and not of Serbs as well. Which is still the case today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And he therefore, did he do nothing to obstruct their return, then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand "no" in the context. Does it mean no he didn't do -- did he do nothing to -- he didn't do nothing so he did something.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not prevent or forbid their return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break. We will come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've got one question for you, Mr. Jarcevic. What, in your view, constitutes a state?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People, territory, and legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That concludes the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, I would like to offer to you a brochure about a short history of Krajina people, to all of you present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will not be necessary. Thanks nonetheless. Mr. Milovancevic, any questions arising from the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Following on from the questions of Judge Nosworthy, sir, isn't it true that at the end of 1992, there was a special session of the RSK assembly and a proposal was made to allow for the return of both Serb and Croatian refugees to Western Slavonia and Mr. Martic and others opposed that proposal saying that the conditions were not right at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite sincerely, I don't remember that session or its conclusions. If you repeat which month it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was at the end of 1992. If you do not know anything about it or if you do not remember, that's fine. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do I take that to understand that you do not remember or you do not know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness had said quite sincerely I don't remember that session or its conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm content to leave it at that. I do have one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware -- and this occurred before you became foreign minister so perhaps you're not aware of it, but are you aware that on the 26th of September 1992, Mr. Martic wrote a letter -- this is in evidence as Exhibit number 232, wrote a letter to the commander of UNPROFOR stating that the RSK government would prevent or resist by force any forced immigration of refugees into the RSK? Are you aware of that letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That position of the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina is familiar to me, but I didn't know that that letter was written by the Minister of the Interior. I reiterate that there was no reciprocity and that had to be our reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally, sir, isn't it true that all during the time that Mr. Martic was Minister of the Interior of the RSK and later as president of the RSK, isn't it true that his position was always that conditions were not right for the return of refugees to the RSK? Wasn't that always his position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JARCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever there was no reciprocity, that was the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Jarcevic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber takes this opportunity to thank you very much for coming to testify in the Tribunal and we hope that you have a safe trip back home and thank you very much once again. You play stand down. You're now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You'll recall that Your Honours, on the 7th of July last week, 2006, it's at transcript 5998, and this was after hearing the request for an extension from the Defence counsel, ordered the Defence to provide detailed 65 ter summaries by today. And I would note that these were 65 ter summaries that should have been provided on the 5th of July. They were not. And the Defence counseled is for a week. It was granted and it was ordered that they be provided today. We have been informed that this is not going to occur today, that they will not be provided until Monday or Tuesday. And I think this is something that, since it's an order of the Court, should be addressed by the Trial Chamber. Secondly -- and our position on that would be that whatever ones have been completed by today should certainly be provided to and then perhaps, we would assent to the remainder being provided by Monday. Secondly, the Court ordered earlier in the week, and this is at 6102, that the Defence provide to the Prosecution all of the documents that were mentioned in the opening statement, and this was after the Defence counsel indicated this could be done by the end of the week. We've also been informed that this will not occur today. And that it will occur as soon as possible with no specific date mentioned. Again, it's an order -- it was ordered by the Trial Chamber so I think it's something that has to be taken up by the Trial Chamber if it's not going to be met today. On that our position is we would certainly assent to those being provided also by Monday of next week. I guess a third point is just I wonder if we could get an indication from the Defence about when -- that we have been told who the first witness will be after the recess. If we could get an indication of when we'll be told of who the witnesses will be after that. It certainly would be of great assistance and preparation and help to ensure that there is no unnecessary delay if we know sooner rather than later which witnesses will be coming first. Even if it's, for example, a list of the first ten witnesses, not necessarily in order but some indication, we have a list of 53 witnesses and it would be very helpful to know, and only a few weeks, it would be very helpful to know where we should start and how to start preparing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any response to those three issues raised by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are working at full bore to fulfil the order of the Trial Chamber to submit a new list of witnesses and witness statements that are now shorter than initially envisaged. We had to go through investigators' notes and it's a very large job of work, and I reckon that we will finish by Monday and I kindly request the Trial Chamber to appreciate the situation. Things stand much the same with the documents and the photograph which is part of those documents. We will submit that. As for witnesses, Your Honour, I wanted to present the position of the Defence in principle. After several months or after a longer time, now when we come to Belgrade, we'll have our first opportunity to talk to the witnesses and I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to give us the opportunity to see whether all of them will remain on the list, whether some of them will testify through 92 bis and we'll submit that list at least a week before resumption of the trial so that you can make your decision on the continuation of the trial. Or rather not the continuation of the trial but the time allowed for the Defence case, I'm sorry for the slip of the tongue. So on this occasion, I do undertake that what we haven't submitted so far we will submit on Monday. I believe that's a deadline that we should be able to comply with. And after talking to the witnesses, we would submit the witness list as I have explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this is clearly not acceptable. I mean, how do you expect your opposite number to work? They must now go and read all 53 witness statements. In fact, even the statements -- you have not even supplied them with the summaries so you are saying they must spend this whole four weeks of recess doing nothing and then they must be ready to start work when we come back. Surely you can give -- Mr. Whiting is saying at least give them a list of your first ten witnesses. You have the list. You know who your witnesses are. You know the order in which you want to call them. Whether you have spoken to them or not, at least you can tell him now who are those witnesses that you intend calling. I don't see why that must wait until just a week before we start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can do that maybe even within the next week, but it's the position of the Defence that we don't want to submit a witness list that is still subject to change because now, in this time which is very short for us, we want to come to arrive at a witness list which would be final. And in this situation, we would like to review the list that the Prosecution has once again to see if some of them can go through 92 bis and some can be eliminated. Of course, we can submit the list of the first ten witnesses before we do the final one; I agree with that but we need some shorter time, at least a week, please, Your Honour. Because that job is waiting for us too. We have to work and work very hard during this holiday and we are in the same situation as our colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you know what? The Chamber appreciates that in a trial, things don't always go according to plan. You might think or decide that you're going to call a certain witness on a certain day, and for completely different reasons beyond your control that witness might not be available but still, this does not mean that you are not in a position to give an indication that, all things going well, I intend calling these witnesses. Okay? There may still be changes. Number 3 might end up being number 6 and number 6 might end up being number 1, but at least you've given a group of witnesses whose statements they can concentrate on during the recess. I'm sure you should be able to do that now. Subject to whatever changes that might come. It happened to them also during the Prosecution case. They used to continuously say, "This is the list. Things might change, but if they don't change that's the list." That's all they are asking for. Can you do that today, ten witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can, Your Honour. Thank you. That's what we'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the documents mentioned in the opening statement, I'm not quite sure I understood your specific answer on that. Now, why is it that you are not able to give them by today? And by when exactly do you think you can give them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all the documents that I mentioned in my opening statement are not on the list of exhibits, the 65 ter list. They are not indicated there as individual documents but they are included in the documents we enumerated as part of some other documents. That's one. So certain documents include the resolution such and such number that I invoked. So in fact, we did submit these documents to the Prosecution. We just need to extract them as individual documents and submit them again. Our most urgent task is to submit those witness statements and that consumes so much of our time that we simply didn't have enough. That's the only reason. And maybe we could provide that on Monday, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see if we can reduce the work for you. You say you did submit those documents but they are part of other documents. Is that -- do I understand you correctly? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If that is the case, is it possible for you to say to the Prosecution, "The documents that we mentioned in our opening statements have been delivered to you, they are part of the following documents. If you go to such and such a bunch of documents at page so and so you'll find this document; at page so and so, you'll find the other document," because it doesn't make sense to give them in duplicate. If you've already given them there is no need for you to give them again but tell them where they are. And I'm sure you would agree with that, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. If I may, I think it may be the case with respect to some of the documents but I don't believe it's the case with respect to all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm giving Mr. Milovancevic the benefit of the doubt that at least those documents that you have given to the Prosecution, just tell them at what pages they are, and you don't have to give extra copies of the same documents. Then they can go and find them there. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How soon can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we do that on Monday, together with the witness statements, to provide it in one package? It's Friday today. End of working hours. On Monday, by the end of working hours, we will submit that. We ourselves want to abide by that deadline. It would mean a lot to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The deadline was for today. Okay. Before I put your proposition to the Prosecution, when you say by Monday, are you saying, all outstanding documents -- when I say outstanding documents, I mean any documents that you mentioned in your opening statement which are not already with the Prosecution will be given by Monday. And the 65 ter summaries? Also by Monday? The detailed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour, correct. That would mean a lot to us to have that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that. I would assent to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, then the orders that were given earlier to say you must file those documents by today are hereby varied by extending the deadline from today to Monday the 17th of July. Now, Mr. Milovancevic, please ensure that by Monday, those detailed summaries are filed and delivered to the Prosecution and that any documents that you mentioned in your opening which are not already part of any disclosures you have made are provided to the Prosecution, and any documents that you mentioned in your opening which are part of previous disclosures, you indicate the pages where they can be found. Those are the three things. Okay? And then the final thing is by Monday, can you please provide the Prosecution with a list of at least ten witnesses that you intend calling as we come back from recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and I thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am just not sure I understand because I thought that had been ordered for today and Defence counsel had agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. That one you have agreed to, to do that today, Mr. Milovancevic. If you can do that today, that would be helpful. Is that okay? Sorry. Are you done with your housekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, while you're on your feet are there any housekeeping matters that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As we go out on recess the Bench just wants to say you have a pleasant what -- are you going to have a holiday, if not a holiday, have a pleasant working time during that period and let's come back refreshed and ready to proceed with the case as expeditiously as we possibly can when we come back on the 14th of August. Court adjourned. May I place it on the transcript, court is adjourned to the 14th of August, in Courtroom II, I'm being advised, at 1415. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.55 p.m.,
